proposed_ruling.headline: Anchoring volume on a market driver at a FLAT share is one-directional on any company that is taking share.
proposed_ruling.plain: We size a company by taking the market it sells into and holding its share of that market steady. For a company whose share has been climbing for years, that is not a neutral assumption — it is a forecast that will be too low every single time, not on average but at every origin. Say the share path out loud and defend it, or accept that the number is a floor and call it one.
proposed_ruling.why: THE FINDING IS ARITHMETIC RATHER THAN STATISTICAL, which is why it is filed at ALL on one name. If share drifts persistently in one direction and the rule holds it flat, the error must be one-directional; nothing about banks or about Egypt is doing the work. Every study in this book anchors volume this way, so the exposure is book-wide. The NARROWER alternative would be CLASS/bank, and it would be filing a property of the rule as though it were a property of banks.
proposed_ruling.overturned: A name where the share of the exogenous market driver has drifted persistently and the mechanical build shows no directional bias — or a market where share is genuinely mean-reverting, in which case the flat-share anchor is right and the drift is the error.

drafts.falsifier: A driver whose forecast error is one-directional across origins and which, on investigation, turns out to have no wiring defect behind it — the error surviving as genuine noise after the model has been read line by line.

drafts.headline: The ecl bias changes direction between regimes.
drafts.plain: It runs one way in one period and the other way in the next. Averaging them produces a correction that is wrong in both. Record it, do not correct for it.
drafts.evidence: By era: E1 recapitalisation and the 2016 float (origins FY2014-FY2017) +0.089; E2 the 2022-24 devaluation sequence (origins FY2018-FY2024) -0.351.

So the scope is the CLASS and not the country: the loss charge is a bank line, and the devaluation is the CONDITION under which the sign flips, not a restriction to Egypt.
drafts.overturned_by: A longer record in which one sign dominates across all regimes.

proposed_ruling.headline: A bank's loss charge is the driver you most want to correct and the one you least may.
proposed_ruling.plain: The provision line is where a bank's profit is decided, so it is the first place anyone reaches for a correction. Do not. Its error changes direction with the credit cycle — too low in one era, too high in the next — so a correction averaged across them is wrong in both. And the currency does not explain it: giving the model perfect foresight of inflation barely moves the miss.
proposed_ruling.why: CLASS rather than ALL because the mechanism is a bank's: a loss charge lags the book that generates it by two or three years, so its error tracks a credit cycle that industrial provisions do not have. CLASS rather than STOCK because the mechanism is not about ADIB — any lender growing a book faster than it seasons it will show the same shape. This is the merge of drafts 12 and 13, which measure two halves of one thing.
proposed_ruling.overturned: A bank whose cost-of-risk bias holds its sign across a full credit cycle, or a decomposition that puts most of a loss-charge error on the macro path.

drafts.falsifier: A bank carried through a devaluation whose loss-charge forecast error keeps the same sign either side of it — the bias not flipping — or one where the average of the two eras produces a correction that improves both.

drafts.headline: For a bank, the cost of funds is divided by the deposits — the industrial rule says exclude them and it inverts.
drafts.plain: The house rule says a borrowing cost is divided by the borrowings that actually bear it, and it names customer deposits as the thing to LEAVE OUT. For a bank that is backwards: depositors are who the bank is paying. Divide the cost of deposits by customers' deposits plus money owed to banks plus subordinated financing, and by nothing wider. The principle travels; the example does not.
drafts.evidence: At ADIB-Egypt's FY2025 the balances that bear the charge are EGP 293.7 billion against total liabilities of EGP 312.1 billion. Reading the industrial rule literally would have excluded customers' deposits — 94% of the correct denominator — and dividing by total liabilities instead understates the funding rate by about a sixth of itself. The build obeys it structurally: bottom_up.interest_bearing() is the only route to that denominator and total liabilities appears nowhere.
drafts.why_scope: Ruled by the principal, 10-09-2026: correct as proposed, banks. Depositors are who the bank pays, so a rule that excludes deposits from the borrowing base inverts the arithmetic for this class alone.
drafts.overturned_by: A deposit-taking institution whose disclosed funding charge is levied on something other than its deposits, bank borrowings and subordinated debt.
drafts.why_not_harvested: lessons_harvest.py reads biases, skill and macro shares. This is a SPECIFICATION finding — a rule read wrongly would have produced a large, robust and entirely spurious bias, and the whole point is that the run avoided producing one. There is no number for the harvester to see, which is exactly why it is proposed by hand and flagged as such.

proposed_ruling.why: CLASS/bank. The inversion is a fact about deposit-taking institutions, and the campaign has now run one. Filing it at ALL would restate the general principle nobody disputes; filing it at STOCK would hide it from the next bank, which is the whole point of writing it down.
proposed_ruling.overturned: A deposit-taking institution whose disclosed funding charge is levied on something other than its deposits, bank borrowings and subordinated debt.

drafts.headline: Apply every rate to the AVERAGE balance sheet. On a fast-growing lender the closing one inflates every projected profit.
drafts.plain: A bank earns its yield on the assets it held through the year, not on the ones it finished with. Put a full year of yield on a closing balance sheet that grew a third and you have credited twelve months of income to assets the bank owned for six. The error is large, it looks like evidence, and it survives every check that does not go looking for it.
drafts.evidence: ADIB-Egypt grew customer financing 54% in FY2025 and total assets 33%, and 19.5% again in the first half of 2026. This is the bank-shaped form of the recognition-clock trap that produced a net-profit forecast several times too high on the first name in this campaign. In this run every rate reaches its base through _avg() and by no other route, which is why the rate drivers came out close to unbiased (net fees 0.984x actual, other income 1.106x, admin 0.897x at the FY2024 origin) while the volume anchor carried the whole miss.
drafts.why_scope: Ruled by the principal, 10-09-2026: correct as proposed, banks. It bites hardest on a fast-growing lender, where a closing balance sheet credits a full year of yield on assets held for part of one.
drafts.overturned_by: A company whose balance sheet grows slowly enough that the average and the closing base give the same answer, in which case the distinction is real and immaterial.
drafts.why_not_harvested: As DRAFT-ADIB-H1: a specification finding leaves no bias behind when it is obeyed, so there is nothing in the score file for the harvester to find. Proposed by hand and flagged.

proposed_ruling.why: CLASS/bank rather than ALL, on the narrower-when-unsure rule. The arithmetic is general — any rate applied to a growing base has it — but the SIZE of the error depends on growing 30-50% a year, which is a lender in a high-inflation economy and not a cement plant.
